# Take a proposal through the governance write flow

In this tutorial you will drive a governance proposal from a captured tension all
the way to acceptance, using the `glassfrog proposal` commands. You will create a
draft proposal, look at it, advance it into circulation, and record a consent
response — and along the way you will see how each step hands you the `prp_` id
and status the next step needs.

By the end you will be able to run the core Holacracy write flow from the command
line: draft a change, circulate it, and let it pass.

## Prerequisites

- The `glassfrog` CLI installed and on your `PATH`.
- A configured API token. If you have not set one up yet, follow the
  authentication tutorial first (`docs/guides/authentication/tutorial.md`) and
  come back once `glassfrog auth login` has stored your credential.
- **An organization with async proposals (Premium) enabled.** The four write
  steps below all require this feature; without it the API answers `403`.
- A captured tension to anchor the proposal to. If you do not have one, capture
  it first with `glassfrog tension create` (see the tensions tutorial).

This tutorial assumes your token is already in place and does not re-teach
authentication.

## Step 1 — Create a draft proposal

A proposal starts as a `draft` anchored to a tension and carrying a set of
governance changes. Pass the anchor tension as the positional argument and the
change set as an inline JSON array:

```
glassfrog proposal create ten_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef \
  --changes '[{"type":"CreateRole","name":"Scribe"}]'
```

The CLI checks only that the change set is valid JSON, non-empty, and that every
element carries a `type` — then sends the array through untouched and lets the
server validate the details. On success it produces the created proposal with its
`prp_` id and `draft` status.

Read that `prp_` id from the output with `-o json`, because every later step
references it:

```
glassfrog proposal create ten_0123…  --changes '[…]' -o json
```

The `data.id` field is the handle you will use from here on.

> A large change set is awkward on the command line. You can instead point
> `--changes` at a file (`--changes changes.json`) or pipe it on standard input
> (`--changes stdin`).

## Step 2 — Look at your proposal

Before circulating, read the proposal back to confirm what it carries:

```
glassfrog proposal get prp_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
```

The single read shows the proposal's `changes` by type, its aggregate
`response_summary`, and — importantly — its `available_transitions`. On a fresh
draft you will see `propose` offered. That list is the server telling you what you
may do next.

You can also see every proposal in flight at once:

```
glassfrog proposal list
```

Narrow it to your own circulating work as you go, for example
`glassfrog proposal list --status proposed_outside_meeting --role-id role_0123…`.

## Step 3 — Advance the proposal into circulation

Advancing a draft starts the consent window — the clock the rest of the flow runs
against. Because the draft offered `propose` in Step 2, you can invoke it:

```
glassfrog proposal propose prp_0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
```

The command sends the transition and lets the server decide — it does not
re-check `available_transitions` first. On success the proposal comes back now in
`proposed_outside_meeting`, carrying a server-set `response_deadline`, your own
implicit `no_objection` already recorded, and an updated transition list (now
offering `withdraw` instead of `propose`).

## Step 4 — Record a consent response

Once a proposal is circulating, each circle member answers it. There are two
answers:

```
glassfrog proposal respond prp_0123…  --response no_objection
```

records that you are willing to let it pass as written. When every expected
responder has answered `no_objection`, the server auto-accepts the proposal — and
the recorded response carries the parent proposal's status as `accepted`, which is
how you know the consent window closed. Read it with `-o json` to catch that
signal:

```
glassfrog proposal respond prp_0123…  --response no_objection -o json
```

If you have a concern instead, answer `--response bring_to_meeting` — that
persists on the proposal and blocks auto-acceptance so the change can be discussed
live. The responding person is always the identity behind your token; you never
name yourself.

## What you've learned

You have run the proposal write flow end to end: created a draft, read its
available transitions, advanced it into circulation, and recorded a response that
can carry the proposal to acceptance. You saw how the `prp_` id and the `status`
field thread the steps together, and that the server — not the CLI — owns the
transitions and the acceptance rule.

From here:

- To re-open a circulating proposal so you can amend it, see
  [How to manage a governance proposal](how-to-manage-a-governance-proposal.md)
  (the `proposal withdraw` task).
- For every flag, filter, and exit code, see the
  [Governance Proposals reference](../../reference/proposals.md).
- To understand *why* the CLI passes change sets through verbatim and never
  pre-checks transitions, see
  [Understanding governance proposals](../../explanation/understanding-governance-proposals.md).
